title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: What is Collective Hysteria?
summary: Playlist episode (SYSK Gets Weird) on collective hysteria, also called mass psychogenic disorder (MPD) or mass psychosomatic reaction. The hosts cover a 2000s-era Mexican girls' boarding school outbreak, the 1998 Tennessee school gas-odor case, the nocebo effect (including the cholecystokinin study and Fabrizio Benedetti's experiment), the New Zealand Loxitane pill-appearance reports, the 1994 Riverside "toxic lady" case, the 2012 Corinth, New York Tourette-like cases, the 1518 Strasbourg dancing plague, and sick building syndrome. They stress that symptoms are real even without a toxic cause, that media coverage and line-of-sight exposure spread it, and that environmental causes must still be ruled out. Listener mail follows near the end, including a note from Jason Flack about his twin sister's death from SUDEP and a request for an epilepsy episode.
topics: Stuff You Should Know Gets Weird playlist

segments.title: Playlist introduction
segments.summary: Host introduces the Stuff You Should Know Gets Weird playlist and this episode on collective hysteria.
topics: Stuff You Should Know Gets Weird playlist

segments.title: Opening banter and diagnosis
segments.summary: Hosts joke around, then introduce collective hysteria, also called mass psychogenic disorder, and discuss why the word hysteria is objectionable.

segments.title: Chalco boarding school outbreak
segments.summary: A 2000-era outbreak among 12 to 17 year old girls at a Catholic boarding school in Chalco, Mexico, with vomiting, walking trouble, fever and nausea, that persisted after a 10-day break. About 600 of 3,600 girls were affected and no environmental cause was found.

segments.title: Definition, history, and gender bias
segments.summary: The hosts note about 80 documented cases and a reported two per week, cite historical examples such as medieval dancing mania and Salem, and discuss why cases skew toward young females, including Ruth Graham's Slate article and a comparison to Beatlemania.

segments.title: Diagnosis pitfalls and risk factors
segments.summary: Physicians must avoid dismissing cases as all in the head, since a British case of tainted cucumbers shows an environmental cause can exist. Outbreaks look like epidemics, and they are more common in isolated, rigidly structured settings such as schools, where between 1973 and 1993 half of outbreaks occurred.

segments.title: Tennessee school gas odor outbreak
segments.summary: A 1998 Tennessee school outbreak began after a teacher noticed a gassy odor. About 180 students and teachers went to the ER, the school closed for two weeks, environmental tests found nothing, and the cause was traced to mass psychogenic disorder. Symptoms typically fade once people are removed from the situation.

segments.title: Nocebo effect and the cholecystokinin study
segments.summary: The hosts define the nocebo effect as the opposite of placebo and discuss a 1886 rose allergy case. They describe research identifying cholecystokinin as involved in nocebo-driven pain, and Fabrizio Benedetti's experiment where blocking it prevented the expected pain increase.

segments.title: Electromagnetic sensitivity and gluten claims
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the film Safe and the case of Debbie Bird, a London woman who says she is allergic to EMF and rewired and shielded her home. They suggest such sensitivities, including claimed gluten sensitivity, may reflect nocebo or collective hysteria.

segments.title: New Zealand Loxitane reports and the nocebo cost
segments.summary: In 2007 New Zealand, reports of side effects for the hormone replacement drug Loxitane rose sharply after the pill's appearance changed, while the active ingredient stayed the same. Media coverage appeared to drive reports. The hosts then discuss the cost of nocebo, including a 1990s study on women who believed they were prone to heart disease.

segments.title: Line of sight exposure and positive attitude
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the power of positive mental attitude, Josh's airplane anecdote about feeling sick after a window shade closed, and how seeing others sick can cause symptoms.

segments.title: Doctors, transparency, and framing side effects
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the ethical problem for physicians of telling patients about possible side effects, since fear is linked to slower healing and infection. Suggested solution is to frame risks positively, and avoid naming illnesses.

segments.title: Corinth New York Tourette cases and Riverside toxic lady
segments.summary: In 2012 in Corinth, New York, a 16-year-old girl named Lori Bronwell lost consciousness at a homecoming dance after headbanging and began showing Tourette-like symptoms; 14 other students were later affected. Erin Brockovich linked it to a 1970 train derailment, but no legitimate effects were found. The hosts then discuss the 1994 Riverside, California toxic lady case, initially called mass hysteria but later linked to a garlic-fruity salve.

segments.title: Sick building syndrome
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sick building syndrome, which may be linked to airtight building design after the OPEC oil embargo and aging ventilation, as well as job dissatisfaction and asthma triggers.

segments.title: Strasbourg dancing plague of 1518
segments.summary: In July 1518, a woman began dancing in Strasbourg, France, and dozens then hundreds joined over weeks; authorities hired musicians, and many died or were injured. Explanations range from ergot poisoning to Sydenham's chorea to mass psychosis. The hosts tie such episodes to beliefs about the devil in earlier times.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts conclude that such episodes come from people being sick of the establishment, and point listeners to the howstuffworks.com search bar.

segments.title: Listener mail: Jason Flack
segments.summary: A listener shares his artwork and tells of losing his twin sister to SUDEP, sudden unexplained death in epilepsy, and asks for an epilepsy episode. The hosts promise to cover epilepsy.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and close the episode.
